etymology: Akkadian Sharru-kin, the true king or he has established the king.
biblical_def: Sargon is the king of Assyria named once in Scripture, in the dating of Isaiah's most startling sign. “In the year that Tartan came unto Ashdod, (when Sargon the king of Assyria sent him,) and fought against Ashdod, and took it” (Isaiah 20:1). That same year the LORD told Isaiah to loose the sackcloth from his loins and put off his shoe, “And he did so, walking naked and barefoot” (Isaiah 20:2), for three years, as “a sign and wonder upon Egypt and upon Ethiopia” (Isaiah 20:3). Judah was tempted to trust Egypt against Assyria; the sign showed that Egypt's captives would be led away naked by the king of Assyria. For centuries Sargon was known only from this verse, and critics doubted him, until the excavation of his palace at Khorsabad in the nineteenth century brought his annals to light, including his campaign against Ashdod. The verse was right all along. The greater lesson is Isaiah's: the coastlands would cry, “whither we flee for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria: and how shall we escape?” (Isaiah 20:6). No earthly ally saves.

pos: n. (proper name; king of Babylon who sent envoys to Hezekiah)
etymology: Akkadian Marduk-apla-iddina, Marduk has given a son; spelled Berodachbaladan in 2 Kings 20:12.
biblical_def: Merodachbaladan is the king of Babylon whose envoys Hezekiah received with fatal pride. “At that time Merodachbaladan, the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a present to Hezekiah: for he had heard that he had been sick, and was recovered” (Isaiah 39:1). The parallel in 2 Kings 20:12 spells him Berodachbaladan. He was a Chaldean prince who fought Assyria for the throne of Babylon and was looking for allies in the west. Hezekiah, flattered, “shewed them the house of his precious things” (Isaiah 39:2) and hid nothing. Isaiah answered with the word of judgment: “Behold, the days come, that all that is in thine house, and that which thy fathers have laid up in store until this day, shall be carried to Babylon: nothing shall be left, saith the LORD” (Isaiah 39:6). A gift from a distant king seemed harmless; it opened the door to the power that would carry Judah away. Hezekiah's reply, “Good is the word of the LORD” (Isaiah 39:8), shows a man humbled, yet content that the evil would not fall in his own days.

pos: n. (proper name; Babylonian chief officer at the fall of Jerusalem)
biblical_def: Nebushasban is one of the princes of Babylon who released Jeremiah after Jerusalem fell. Nebuchadrezzar had given charge concerning the prophet: “Take him, and look well to him, and do him no harm” (Jeremiah 39:12). “So Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard sent, and Nebushasban, Rabsaris, and Nergalsharezer, Rabmag, and all the king of Babylon's princes” (Jeremiah 39:13), and “took Jeremiah out of the court of the prison, and committed him unto Gedaliah” (Jeremiah 39:14). Rabsaris is his title, chief officer, the head of the court eunuchs. His name prayed to a Babylonian god for deliverance, yet he became the instrument of the true God's deliverance of His prophet. The men of Judah had imprisoned Jeremiah for speaking God's word; the pagan officers of the conqueror set him free. God keeps His word to His servants, even by the hands of those who do not know Him.

pos: n. (proper name; founder of the Aramean kingdom of Damascus)
etymology: Hebrew Rezon, prince, ruler, from razan, to be weighty, to rule.
biblical_def: Rezon is the adversary God raised against Solomon in Damascus. “And God stirred him up another adversary, Rezon the son of Eliadah, which fled from his lord Hadadezer king of Zobah” (1 Kings 11:23). When David defeated Zobah, Rezon escaped with a band of men, went to Damascus, “and dwelt therein, and reigned in Damascus” (1 Kings 11:24). “And he was an adversary to Israel all the days of Solomon, beside the mischief that Hadad did: and he abhorred Israel, and reigned over Syria” (1 Kings 11:25). The point of the narrative is the cause: Solomon's heart had turned after other gods, and the LORD who had given him rest on every side now stirred up enemies. First Hadad the Edomite, then Rezon of Damascus. The kingdom of Syria that would trouble Israel for two centuries began as God's rod against a king who forsook Him. Rezon did not rise by chance; God stirred him up.

pos: n. (proper name; king of Damascus, father of Benhadad I)
etymology: Aramaic Tabrimmon, Rimmon is good, honoring the Syrian god Rimmon.
biblical_def: Tabrimon is the king of Syria whose son Asa hired against Israel. “King Asa sent them to Benhadad, the son of Tabrimon, the son of Hezion, king of Syria, that dwelt at Damascus” (1 Kings 15:18), with the silver and gold of the house of the LORD. Asa's message invoked an old treaty: “There is a league between me and thee, and between my father and thy father” (1 Kings 15:19). The father so invoked was Tabrimon. Benhadad broke his league with Baasha and struck the northern cities, and Asa's plan seemed to succeed. But Hanani the seer rebuked him: “Because thou hast relied on the king of Syria, and not relied on the LORD thy God, therefore is the host of the king of Syria escaped out of thine hand” (2 Chronicles 16:7). The name Tabrimon praises an idol; the league with his house cost Judah the treasures of the temple and earned the rebuke of God. A king who had once trusted the LORD against a million Ethiopians now trusted Damascus.

pos: n. (proper name; father of the puppet king planned for Judah)
etymology: Aramaic Tab'el, God is good; the Masoretic pointing Tabe'al has been read as a play, good for nothing.
biblical_def: Tabeal is named as the father of the man Syria and Ephraim meant to set on David's throne. Rezin and Pekah conspired against Ahaz, saying, “Let us go up against Judah, and vex it, and let us make a breach therein for us, and set a king in the midst of it, even the son of Tabeal” (Isaiah 7:6). They “have taken evil counsel against thee” (Isaiah 7:5), the LORD told Ahaz, and called the two kings “two tails of these smoking firebrands” (Isaiah 7:4). The son of Tabeal is not even given his own name. God's answer was brief: “It shall not stand, neither shall it come to pass” (Isaiah 7:7). The plot struck at the covenant with David, which promised a son of David on the throne forever. Into that crisis God gave the sign of Immanuel. The son of Tabeal was the world's candidate; the virgin's Son was God's.

pos: n. (proper name; an official who wrote against the Jews)
biblical_def: Tabeel is one of the officials who wrote to the king of Persia against the rebuilding of Jerusalem. “And in the days of Artaxerxes wrote Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel, and the rest of their companions, unto Artaxerxes king of Persia; and the writing of the letter was written in the Syrian tongue” (Ezra 4:7). He belonged to the people of the land who resisted the returned exiles: “Then the people of the land weakened the hands of the people of Judah, and troubled them in building” (Ezra 4:4). The campaign of letters succeeded for a time: “Then ceased the work of the house of God which is at Jerusalem” (Ezra 4:24). Tabeel's name confesses that God is good, while his pen was turned against God's house. Opposition to the work of God often comes dressed in official correspondence and legal process. Yet the work resumed under Haggai and Zechariah, and the house was finished. He is distinct from Tabeal of Isaiah 7.

pos: n. (proper name; an envoy who asked about the fasts)
etymology: Hebrew Regem Melek, friend of the king or the king's spokesman.
biblical_def: Regemmelech is one of the envoys sent to the priests and prophets to ask whether the fasts of mourning should continue. “When they had sent unto the house of God Sherezer and Regemmelech, and their men, to pray before the LORD” (Zechariah 7:2), they asked, “Should I weep in the fifth month, separating myself, as I have done these so many years?” (Zechariah 7:3). The fifth-month fast mourned the burning of the temple, and now the temple was being rebuilt. God answered with a searching question: “When ye fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh month, even those seventy years, did ye at all fast unto me, even to me?” (Zechariah 7:5). The LORD then named what He required: “Execute true judgment, and shew mercy and compassions every man to his brother” (Zechariah 7:9). Regemmelech came with a question of ritual; he received a word about the heart. In Zechariah 8 God promised that the fasts would become feasts of joy.

biblical_def: Mehuman heads the list of the seven chamberlains whom Ahasuerus sent for Vashti. “On the seventh day, when the heart of the king was merry with wine, he commanded Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, and Abagtha, Zethar, and Carcas, the seven chamberlains that served in the presence of Ahasuerus the king” (Esther 1:10), “To bring Vashti the queen before the king with the crown royal, to shew the people and the princes her beauty” (Esther 1:11). Vashti refused, “therefore was the king very wroth, and his anger burned in him” (Esther 1:12). Mehuman carried a drunken king's command and returned with a refusal that cost a queen her crown. The episode opened the way for Esther. Mehuman's brief appearance belongs to the hidden providence that runs through the whole book: the name of God is never mentioned, yet a feast, a refusal and a royal decree all move toward the deliverance of His people.

pos: n. (proper name; one of the seven princes of Persia and Media)
etymology: Persian, of uncertain meaning; perhaps worthy or noble.
biblical_def: Marsena is one of the seven princes of Persia and Media who counselled Ahasuerus after Vashti's refusal. The king turned to “the wise men, which knew the times” (Esther 1:13). “And the next unto him was Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven princes of Persia and Media, which saw the king's face, and which sat the first in the kingdom” (Esther 1:14). The king asked, “What shall we do unto the queen Vashti according to law” (Esther 1:15), and Memucan, speaking for the council, proposed that it “be written among the laws of the Persians and the Medes, that it be not altered, That Vashti come no more before king Ahasuerus” (Esther 1:19). Marsena sat among the highest men of the empire, yet the counsel of all seven served a purpose none of them knew. The vacancy they created was filled by a Jewish orphan. The unalterable law of the Medes and Persians would later bind the king again, and God would overrule it too.

The name appears once, in Esther 1:14.
He was one of the seven princes who saw the king's face.
The council advised the deposing of Vashti.
The princes sat first in the kingdom.
scriptures: Est 1:13
Then the king said to the wise men, which knew the times, (for so was the king's manner toward all that knew law and judgment:
Est 1:14
And the next unto him was Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven princes of Persia and Media, which saw the king's face, and which sat the first in the kingdom;)
Est 1:15
What shall we do unto the queen Vashti according to law, because she hath not performed the commandment of the king Ahasuerus by the chamberlains?
Est 1:19

If it please the king, let there go a royal commandment from him, and let it be written among the laws of the Persians and the Medes, that it be not altered, That Vashti come no more before king Ahasuerus; and let the king give her royal estate unto another that is better than she.
corruption_summary: The counsel of the powerful is trusted as final; Marsena and the seven princes served a providence they did not see.
corruption_paragraphs: The wise men of Persia knew the times and the law, but not the God who rules them. Human counsel, however high, is never ultimate.
This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the king's heart and the counsel of his princes are in the hand of the LORD.
roots_summary: Persian, perhaps noble; one of the seven princes of Persia and Media.
roots_lines: Persian name of uncertain meaning.
One of the seven princes (Esther 1:14).
They saw the king's face and sat first in the kingdom.
Their counsel deposed Vashti.
Their decree was written among the unalterable laws.
